doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

title: Admiring his father's dedication and limits as a show player
summary: What impressed him about being hired was his father's busy phone and daily practice; his father could not read shows.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: When was your first — did you have a time, place or person that you felt was really a significant gig in this early, you were what in your late teens or early twenties? Was there something that came up at that time that, boy, this is really important?

I think it’s because I did respect my father and what he did. The phone would ring all the time and for someone just to call you up and hire you, and think enough of your craft to employ you, impressed me. Because I would ask my mother, what’s going on here? And

she explained it to me, well these people are having weddings, concerts, music lessons, and they’re calling for your dad. And that impressed me about it. And it impressed me how dedicated he was because he would get up every morning and practice for a couple of hours. And he knew tunes, he knew jazz tunes, he would work at them, practice for hours, and did until the day he passed on.
And so he was the kind of musician that, much like yourself, could function in a lot of different settings. As you mentioned, versatility.

He could, yes. He wasn’t a show player, and that’s probably why he got me in that situation. He says just listen, you can push it through. But I couldn’t. You can’t. And sooner or later I think everybody that tries it, I’ve seen it with students come back to me, who have gotten into a situation where they think they can do a show and the conductor has them for lunch. And it doesn’t work, and they come back, and they say please, put on the shine, what can I do? You know he couldn’t read because he was legally blind.
